title: WHO Depression Evidence Snapshot
content:
Depression involves depressed mood or loss of pleasure or interest in activities for prolonged periods. A depressive episode differs from ordinary mood fluctuations. Symptoms occur most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks, and may include poor concentration, excessive guilt or low self-worth, hopelessness, thoughts about dying or suicide, sleep disruption, appetite or weight changes, and low energy. Depression can impair functioning at home, work, school, and in the community.

Depression can be categorized as mild, moderate, or severe according to the number and severity of symptoms and their effect on functioning. Depressive disorders can occur as a single episode or recurrent disorder, and depressive episodes can also occur in bipolar disorder, where periods of mania or hypomania are relevant to the clinical assessment.

Effective treatments for depression include psychological treatments and medicines. Psychological treatments include behavioural activation, cognitive behavioural therapy, interpersonal psychotherapy, and problem-solving therapy. For moderate and severe depression, psychological treatment may be combined with antidepressant medication. Treatment choices should consider adverse effects, availability of the intervention, and individual preferences.

People with depression can have thoughts about dying or suicide. Clinical care should take these symptoms seriously and connect people to appropriate professional support. Depression is treatable, and urgent help is appropriate when there is immediate danger of self-harm.

title: NICE Depression in Adults Evidence Snapshot
source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
content:
NICE guidance for adults with depression emphasizes assessment of symptoms, functioning, risks, comorbidities, previous treatment, and the person's preferences and circumstances when planning care.

Treatment selection for depression should take account of clinical presentation, severity, patient preference, previous treatment and response, comorbidities, risks and benefits, and availability. Shared decision-making is part of treatment planning.

During treatment, regular review is used to assess response, adverse effects, adherence, emerging risks, and whether the treatment plan needs adjustment. Review frequency should reflect the treatment and the person's clinical circumstances and level of risk.

When depression has not improved, assessment should revisit the diagnosis, comorbidities, adherence, adequacy of the treatment, adverse effects, psychosocial factors, and available further treatment options. Treatment-resistant depression requires a structured review rather than assuming that one intervention has failed in isolation.

After recovery, continued treatment may be considered when relapse risk is significant. Decisions about continuation or maintenance should consider previous episodes, relapse risk, treatment response, patient preference, and the balance of benefits and harms.

Early treatment changes should be interpreted in clinical context. Follow-up should review symptom trajectory, adverse effects, activation or worsening symptoms, adherence, and safety rather than assuming that every early change represents improvement or deterioration.
